extracted.intended_audience: reporters, copy editors, and newsroom editors (especially police/court/city-hall reporters and sports reporters)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and practical rules for producing legally safe, clear, and mechanically workable local news copy — especially police, court, legislative, and hurried 'sectional' stories — plus guidance on federal publication limits and sports-reporting focus. Emphasizes libel/privilege law, contempt, federal prohibitions, copyright, and newsroom sectional-story technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute extra-record statements to source
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting information that goes beyond the documented, official record (ex parte or unofficial statements), attribute it directly to its source (e.g., police) and emphasize that it is the view or belief of that source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Use wording such as "Police declare" or "Lieut. Mahoney said" to show good faith. Attribution softens possible libel but does not automatically remove it; it shows information was obtained without malicious intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid presenting unofficial/opinionated police statements as facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not present the prejudiced or ex parte statements of police as established fact when those statements go beyond the official record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the paper prints the police's prejudiced reasons for an arrest and the arrest proves an error, the paper may be liable. Best practice is to attribute such statements and avoid asserting them as proven facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualify doubtful identifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Any doubtful identification (e.g., identity shown only by a borrowed permit/registration) should be given in qualified form rather than printed as definitive fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example phrasing: "The driver identified himself as John Doe, 211 Zero Street." This protects against mistaken identification suits when IDs can be borrowed or misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court reporting must be accurate, impartial, and complete
rubrics_metrics.description: Material that genuinely is before a court may be reported safely provided the reporting is accurate, impartial, and complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A case is considered 'before the court' when the judge begins consideration; state rules differ (e.g., New York and Kentucky treat filing as sufficient; many other states require judge action). Be sure the matter was actually in the official record before publishing detailed allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish only what is in the official record for privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: Conditional privilege attaches to anything admitted into the official court record; testimony or statements expunged or ordered stricken are not privileged and should not be printed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Printing testimony that a judge has ordered expunged is equivalent to proclaiming material the judge ruled never had been uttered and may expose the paper to liability (and contempt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney statements privileged only if relevant/'on the track'
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements by attorneys are conditionally privileged if they are relevant to the case or 'on the track'; irrelevant attorney tirades about nonparties are not protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A lawyer's vivid attack on a non-involved third party may be printed at the paper's risk because it is unrelated to the proceedings and hard to defend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative and official acts are conditionally privileged; unofficial remarks are not
rubrics_metrics.description: Public actions and utterances made in the course of legislative or official duties are generally conditionally privileged; what officials say off the record or when not acting officially has no privilege.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A city council member's remarks during an official meeting are privileged; the same official's remarks afterward on a private stroll are not. The definition of 'legislature' includes bodies empowered to make rules binding on the public (state assemblies, county boards, city councils).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public deliberations of private groups lack privilege unless high public concern
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberations of private groups are generally without privilege even if their work affects the public, unless court decisions recognize conditional privilege for matters of high public importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A real-estate brokers' organization's expulsion may be treated without privilege; reporter should consult editors before publishing such material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair comment limited to public acts or works, not personal attacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment is not libelous if legally 'fair' — i.e., limited to criticism of the work or actions that the person has offered to the public; personal attacks or imputations of motive risk libel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Calling an architect's plan 'ludicrous' is permissible if the plan was offered publicly; accusing the architect personally of theft is different and may be actionable. Criticism of official actions is protected; asserting corrupt motives requires proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prejudicial commentary while a case is in progress (contempt risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not publish commentary about an ongoing case that might influence witnesses or jurors; wait until the case is ended to write evaluative comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of forbidden commentary: asserting that a witness 'made a monkey of himself' which may intimidate later witnesses. Printing stricken testimony is also contempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not print testimony stricken from the record
rubrics_metrics.description: Material the judge orders expunged from the record must not be printed; printing it constitutes contempt of court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if obtained legitimately, once testimony is stricken it is treated as never having been uttered and is unprivileged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not publish names of lottery/sweepstakes winners where federal law forbids
rubrics_metrics.description: Naming winners of sweepstakes or products of lotteries may break Federal law; papers should avoid publishing such names when the promotion is a lottery under law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal law treats games where payment is required and outcome is by chance as lotteries; printing names of winners of such promotions can violate the law and FCC/postal rules may be involved with sweepstakes, especially foreign ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not present non-government predictions as official weather reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid publishing weather predictions or forecasts made by anyone other than a government meteorologist in a way that could be mistaken for an official forecast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The government has a monopoly on weather forecasts because of their potential consequences for farmers, mariners, and businesses; reporters should not substitute amateur forecasts for official ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid printing images of money, postage stamps, or citizenship papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not print pictures of currency, postage stamps, or citizenship papers because reproductions might aid counterfeiters or lead to misuse of engraving plates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The government forbids even remote risks of misuse; refrain from reproductions of these specific items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid indecency and restrict profanity in text
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove indecent material from publication; profanity and blasphemy are deleted even when quoted from testimony; only mild expletives such as 'hell' and 'damn' are reserved for rare, special occasions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial judgment required: indecency standards are not categorical, but remove sexual indecency and strong profanities from copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid incitement to sedition; wartime standards may be stricter
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not publish material intended to incite overthrow of the government or give aid to enemies; reporting on radical meetings is generally acceptable if presented impartially and not to provoke violence, but wartime sensitivities may change the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Reporting that speakers shouted 'The government's all wrong' is usually newsworthy; publishing material intended to provoke violence could be seditious particularly during wartime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious using police radio material and do not reveal radio as source
rubrics_metrics.description: Information taken from police radio transmissions may contravene FCC regulations; if used, reporters customarily avoid mentioning the radio as the source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters often get the same information at the station so trouble is rare, but occasional unique radio-only items pose legal/regulatory risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid infringing copyrighted material; crediting is not a defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not reproduce copyrighted material so completely that it impedes sales of the original; simply crediting the source (e.g., 'as copyrighted by the Journal') does not avoid infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Lifting a scoop from another paper and announcing their copyright can still be infringement; assess substantiality and market effect before republishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: When writing hurried/sectional stories, write simply and directly
rubrics_metrics.description: In 'hurry-up' sectional reporting, reporters should set aside stylistic embellishments and write straightforward English, drawing power from directness rather than glittering phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dave planned the story on the drive back and wrote correctly the first time because there was no time for polishing; avoid complex phrasing that slows production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a consistent slugline/identification for all sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Label each fragment of a sectional story with the same identification (slugline) so the copy desk and composing room can assemble parts in the correct sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Use 'Mayor' for all parts rather than varying slugs like 'Mayor', 'Vote', 'Council' — consistent slug prevents the composing room from treating parts as separate stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number sections sequentially and do not skip numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign sequential 'Add 1', 'Add 2' etc. numbers to each section and be punctilious about arithmetic; skipping or omitting a number causes confusion and lost time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reporter jumps from 'Add 6' to 'Add 8', the composing room will hunt for the missing 'Add 7' and valuable minutes will be lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: End each section at a paragraph boundary (never mid-paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: Always end a sectional fragment at the conclusion of a paragraph to avoid awkward typesetting and broken lines when the composing room assembles the parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Add 9 ends mid-paragraph and Add 10 starts the continuation, assembled type may look odd and signal an error to printers and editors; avoid by closing each fragment at a paragraph end.

rubrics_metrics.name: When lead will arrive later, label parts to indicate 'lead to come' and insertion instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reporter writes the body before the lead is known, use clear labels like 'Add Wreck — Lead to Come', 'Pick Up Early', 'Precede', and give explicit insertion instructions for later additions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example labels: 'Lead Wreck', 'Add 1 Lead Wreck', 'Pick Up Add Wreck'; for last-minute death updates, write a short 'Precede' blurb to run in front of the earlier copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mark proofs and use 'insert' labels with clear placement directions
rubrics_metrics.description: Mark each section for proof (e.g., 'Proof to Johnson'); when splicing new information use 'Insert A', 'Insert B' and specify exactly (e.g., 'Insert A Wreck, after 4th pgh., "the coroner said"').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no proof is available, provide specific placement directions referencing paragraph content or number so the copy desk can place the insert correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize wholesale proof changes; make new copy fit existing space
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid asking to replace whole types when proofs are already set because resetting type is slow; when a genuine change is needed, try to make the new phrasing fit the original space so only minimal adjustments are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: If correcting 'Elon' to 'Ellington' overflows the first line, adjust following lines to compensate rather than recasting the entire paragraph unnecessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write sectional paragraphs as independent blocks (avoid strong transitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid linking paragraphs with transitions like 'Meanwhile' or 'However'; make each paragraph a self-contained block so mis-sequencing in assembly does not garble the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces damage when composing room assembles sections out of sequence, especially when apprentices are on make-up duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports reporters must develop local specialties beyond the 'big four'
rubrics_metrics.description: Because sports reporting is crowded, sports writers should cultivate knowledge of the specialties popular in their city (e.g., hockey, polo) rather than relying solely on generic knowledge of football/baseball/basketball/boxing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors expect specialized local knowledge; national games are usually covered by wire services, so a local reporter's value lies in home-grown or specialty sports coverage.
